title: INT Data Types (BIGINT, INT, SMALLINT, TINYINT)
description: Learn about SQL Server integer data types and how to use them effectively.

data.text: SQL Server supports standard SQL integer types including BIGINT, INT, SMALLINT, and TINYINT. Choose the smallest type that can reliably contain all possible values.

data.title: Create Table with Integer Columns
data.content: Creates a table with all four integer types and inserts maximum values.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE test.sql_server_integers (
    bigint_col bigint,
    int_col INT,
    smallint_col SMALLINT,
    tinyint_col tinyint
);

INSERT INTO test.sql_server_integers (
    bigint_col,
    int_col,
    smallint_col,
    tinyint_col
)
VALUES (
    9223372036854775807,
    2147483647,
    32767,
    255
);

data.text: SQL Server converts integer constants greater than 2,147,483,647 to DECIMAL data type, not BIGINT.

data.title: Integer Division Behavior
data.content: Shows how integer division changes type when threshold is exceeded.

data.text: Integer division in T-SQL truncates toward zero, and mixing an integer with a decimal promotes the result to decimal. The script below shows both behaviours plus the classic overflow problem: two values that each fit in INT but whose sum does not.

data.title: Truncation, promotion, and overflow
data.content: The final statement would raise `Arithmetic overflow error converting expression to data type int` if the values were summed as INT, so cast the first operand to BIGINT.
data.code:
SELECT
    7 / 2                     AS truncated,   -- 3
    7.0 / 2                   AS promoted,    -- 3.500000
    7 % 2                     AS remainder;    -- 1

DECLARE @big INT = 2147483647;
SELECT CAST(@big AS BIGINT) + 1 AS safe_sum;      -- 2147483648

data.title: Interview answer
data.text: Mention that IDENTITY/primary keys are usually INT and that 2,147,483,647 is a hard ceiling — high-volume tables should use BIGINT for their identity key, or the counter can wrap and break the application. Also say that `SUM()` over an INT column returns INT, so it can overflow in a report even when every individual row is fine.

data.title: Integer Types Key Points
points: Use the smallest integer type that can reliably contain all possible values.
TINYINT is sufficient for small ranges (0-255).
INT is the most commonly used integer type.
BIGINT is needed for very large values.
SQL Server converts large integer constants to DECIMAL, not BIGINT.
